title: Shoot Multiplication, Organogenesis and Genotype Response

content.overview: Cannabis tissue culture includes axillary shoot multiplication and de-novo regeneration pathways such as direct organogenesis. These approaches differ in scalability, fidelity risk and genotype sensitivity, so protocol choice should follow the biological goal.

vocabulary.definition: Propagation through pre-existing shoot meristems or nodes.
Regeneration of organs such as shoots from cultured tissue.
A proliferating mass of relatively undifferentiated plant cells that can arise in culture.

sections.title: Multiplication rate is not the only quality metric
sections.body: A treatment that produces more shoots may also change shoot length, callus formation or later rooting performance. Recent cannabis work found such tradeoffs with plant-growth-regulator treatments.

sections.title: Regeneration routes have different uses
sections.body: Direct organogenesis and callus-associated regeneration can increase multiplication capacity and support biotechnology, but they may carry different fidelity and reproducibility considerations than simple nodal multiplication.

sections.title: Cultivar response must be measured
sections.body: Recent studies report cultivar-dependent tissue-culture performance. A robust program compares genotypes under defined conditions rather than declaring one recipe universally optimal.

workedExamples: A regulator treatment that doubles shoot count but increases basal callus should be evaluated for downstream quality, not ranked by shoot number alone.
If a regeneration method performs well on one cultivar and poorly on another, record that as genotype interaction rather than protocol failure alone.
commonMistakes: Assuming one cultivar validates a universal protocol.
Ignoring callus formation or abnormal morphology during selection.
content.practicalApplication: Compare treatments with a scorecard including multiplication rate, shoot length, node number, callus, abnormal morphology, rooting success and genotype.
content.summary: Advanced multiplication is a multi-trait optimization problem. Genotype, explant, medium and regulators interact, so quality and downstream performance matter as much as shoot count.
